title: Teach Well and Blue Haven Primary School
author: Sue Knight
summary: Knight closes a four part account of a ten day school visiting tour with a day at Blue Haven Public School, a New South Wales school at the seventeenth percentile of socio-educational advantage that posted rapid NAPLAN growth between 2016 and 2018 and has held it since. Her report is observational rather than argumentative, cataloguing tight routines, calm rooms, fast paced review and staff who can explain the how and why of their teaching at a fine level of detail. She reads the visit against William Louden's 2015 study of high performing Western Australian primary schools and finds all three of his common characteristics present, namely stable long term leadership, developed improvement plans and early synthetic phonics. A second frame comes from Robert Pondiscio on what makes school success durable, where structured curriculum, shared materials and a culture that survives staff turnover matter more than innovation or technology. Knight is careful about context, quoting a social media post on the different daily experience of leading in affluent and high poverty communities while refusing to let that difference become a reason to subordinate teaching to wellbeing. The installment ends with tips seventeen through twenty for leaders, on daily classroom conversations, using rather than displaying data, sourcing ideas from schools further ahead, and holding urgency and patience together. The full twenty tip list is reproduced at the close, which makes this the summary document for the whole series.
points: Knight treats Blue Haven as a test of whether documented gains hold, noting the 2016 to 2018 case study growth is still embedded seven years on and that staff pictured in it remain at the school.

She matches the visit against Louden's three common characteristics of high performing primary schools and finds all of them present, including stable long term leadership and early synthetic phonics.

The leadership advice she collects from principal Dale Edwards is deliberately unglamorous, centred on leaving the office, leading professional learning personally and getting into classrooms to see the work.
She reports the deputy principal's stance on data as never treating the school as having arrived, and argues the relentless use rather than display of data is what moves successful schools forward.
The final four tips address leaders directly and end on a deliberate contradiction, that school improvement requires both a sense of urgency and patience with how long it takes.
quotes: There is a huge spread of knowledge between schools. Some are a long way along the evidence-informed journey and others are just starting. Teach Well have a great saying ‘any amount more.’ Just get better, one step at a time.
It is truly a privilege when teachers put their hands up to host visitors from outside their school. This requires a high level of trust and a commitment to improvement beyond their own school.

Jess and I saw tight routines, calm classrooms, fast paced reviews with students reciting, recalling and applying their knowledge, confident and skilled teachers, learning as the focus, minimal or no disruptions, and a team able to articulate the how and why of teaching to the micro level of detail.

I thought of that research while we were walking around Blue Haven as the same three characteristics that Louden found in his research were evident at Blue Haven: stable long-term school leadership; well-developed school improvement plans; and reading programs based on explicit teaching of synthetic phonics in the early years.
The relentless focus on data, both fine grained and big picture, and being aspirational with data – never thinking we are ‘there’ – drives successful schools and leadership teams forward.

I asked Dale what his advice to other leaders would be and again it aligns with what other instructional leaders at high performing schools say: roll up your sleeves and get out of your office; have deep and rich conversations about research and what that looks like on the ground; lead PL and if others lead it, share your commitment and understanding; get into classrooms and see it – see the work being done.

Tip#17: Have daily conversations about what’s happening in classrooms. If you spend a day as a leader talking and thinking about other things (and that can absolutely happen) as soon as you can, snap your attention back to teaching and learning.

Tip #18: Learn to love data - screening, diagnostic, progress monitoring, and outcomes. USE data, don’t just collate and display it. Accept where you are (don’t deny or hide it) and if it’s not good enough and not where you want your school to be, commit to not staying there.
